newsitem.title: ITALY: Thousands demonstrate in Rome against unemployment.
newsitem.headline: Thousands demonstrate in Rome against unemployment.

text.p: Tens of thousands of people poured through the streets of Rome on Saturday in a colourful union demonstration called to demand concerted government action to cut Italy's army of unemployed.

Three huge columns of protesters brought large parts of the capital to a standstill as they converged on a huge square infront of Rome's St John's cathedral where the leaders of Italy's three main union federations addressed the crowd.
"A country is only civilised if it is able to provide work for its young and protection for the weak," said Sergio Cofferati, head of the largest labour movement, the Cgil.

Latest data from October last year said 12.2 percent of the workforce was without a job, but there were large regional differences, with the unemployment rate in the south over 21 percent against just 7.1 percent for the north.
Youth unemployment stood at nearly 35 percent.
Prime Minister Romano Prodi's centre-left government introduced a raft of measures on Friday aimed at boosting employment, especially in the underdeveloped south.

Among the initiatives approved by the cabinet and put immediately into affect by decree, were the release of up to 12 trillion lire ($7.1 billion) of funds mainly aimed at job creation schemes for the south.
The government also introduced new regulations to help unblock major public work projects which ground to a halt in the early 1990s following nationwide corruption probes.
Unions welcomed the decree, but said more must be done.

"The government has finally started to move thanks to our demonstration today. But this initiative is still far from bearing fruit," said Sergio D'Antoni, leader of Italy's second largest union grouping, the Cisl.
More than 2,000 special trains and coaches brought people from around Italy to Saturday's march. Unions said the crowd numbered around 400,000 but police said it was nearer 150,000.
A sea of red, green and white union flags were held aloft, with protesters chanting a single slogan: "work, work"
One student held up a placard with the slogan: "We need new dreams tonight", while a union group had a huge banner reading: "Prodi, what a disappointment".
Prodi put employment at the top of his agenda when he took office 10 months ago, but unions complain he has since dragged his feet and has not fully implemented a labour accord signed last September.
The "pact for jobs", agreed with both unions and employers, included a reduction in the working week, incentives for people starting their own businesses and tax breaks on research.
Massimo D'Alema, head of the largest coalition party, the Democratic Party of the Left (PDS), joined Saturday's protest, saying that it was not an anti-government rally.

"This (march) is a type of stimulus, a request for commitment to focus on the battle for the creation of new jobs, especially in the south," D'Alema said in a letter published in Il Messaggero newspaper on Saturday. $1 = 1,690 lire
